# Insurance (marine, fire, life) (`insurance`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by probability_statistics, life_tables_annuities, double_entry
- Core idea: Many people who face the same risk each pay a small premium into a pool, and the few who suffer the loss are paid out of it. It works because among many independent ships or houses the share lost each year is predictable even though no single loss is: the law of large numbers. Premium = expected loss + costs + margin, so the insurer needs records of how often ships sink or houses burn. Spread each risk among several underwriters, keep reserves, insure no more than the true value, and make the insured bear part of the loss so that he still takes care (deductible, co-insurance); inspect ships and houses and ask about health so that only bad risks are not the ones who buy.
- Pitfalls:
  - Insuring risks that strike all at once (a whole town burning, war, epidemic): the pool fails exactly when needed
  - Insuring a ship or house above its value invites scuttling and arson
  - Charging everyone the same premium: the young and safe leave, the old and risky stay, and the pool goes bankrupt (adverse selection)
  - Allowing policies on strangers' lives: it becomes betting and a motive for murder; require an insurable interest
  - Repeating the unsourced claim that Chinese merchants in the 3rd millennium BC insured by spreading cargo over many boats
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1754 BC – Hammurabi §§100–103: a trading agent robbed on the road swears an oath and is released from repaying the investor, an allocation of risk rather than insurance; greece: 4th c. BC – maritime loans (bottomry): repaid with high interest only if the ship arrives, combining credit and insurance; rome: fenus nauticum (sea loan); burial clubs (collegia) pay members' funerals from dues; islamic: the aqila, a kin group sharing blood-money payments, is a mutual liability rule, not commercial insurance; Muslim jurists debated commercial insurance from the 19th c. (Ibn Abidin); europe: 1347 – Genoa, earliest known separate marine insurance contracts (premium paid, no loan); 1435 Barcelona insurance ordinance; c. 1688 Lloyd's coffee house in London; 1676 Hamburg's public fire fund; 1680 Barbon's Fire Office after the 1666 fire; 1762 Equitable Society with age-graded life premiums; americas: 1752 – Philadelphia Contributionship fire insurance (Franklin)
- Read:
  - Florence Edler de Roover, Early Examples of Marine Insurance, Journal of Economic History 5 (1945)
  - Peter L. Bernstein, Against the Gods: The Remarkable Story of Risk (1996)
  - Geoffrey Clark, Betting on Lives: The Culture of Life Insurance in England, 1695–1775 (1999)
